Active snap trap, native to the Carolinas

The Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) is perhaps the most famous carnivorous plant in the world. Its leaves have evolved into a hinged trap mechanism that snaps shut when trigger hairs are touched twice in quick succession, trapping unsuspecting prey. It is native to the subtropical wetlands of North and South Carolina.
Subtropical wetlands of North and South Carolina, USA
Active snap trap – triggered by sensitive hairs on trap lobes
North American pitcher plant with tubular leaves

Sarracenia, the North American pitcher plants, form elegant tubular leaves that act as pitfall traps. Insects are lured in by colorful patterns, nectar, and scent. Once inside, downward-pointing hairs and slippery waxy surfaces prevent escape, and digestive enzymes break down the prey into nutrients.
Bogs and fens of eastern North America
Pitfall trap – tubular leaf filled with digestive fluid

Nepenthes, the tropical pitcher plants, form the largest genus of carnivorous plants. Their pendulous pitchers dangle from tendrils at the tips of leaves. The pitchers contain a viscoelastic digestive fluid that traps and digests everything from small insects to occasionally small vertebrates like frogs and even rats.
Tropical rainforests of Southeast Asia, especially Borneo and Sumatra
Pitfall trap – hanging pitcher with slippery peristome rim

Drosera, commonly known as sundews, is one of the largest genera of carnivorous plants with over 190 species. Their leaves are covered with reddish tentacles tipped with glistening droplets of sticky mucilage resembling dewdrops. Insects landing on the leaf are caught fast, and the tentacles curl inward to maximize digestion.
Every continent except Antarctica, from bogs to tropical savannas
Flypaper trap – adhesive mucilage on tentacles with active movement

Utricularia, or bladderworts, are the largest genus of carnivorous plants and possess the most sophisticated trapping mechanism in the plant kingdom. Their tiny bladder-shaped traps maintain negative internal pressure. When trigger hairs are touched, the trapdoor opens and the prey is sucked in within milliseconds — one of the fastest movements in the plant world.
Aquatic and semi-aquatic environments on every continent
Suction trap – ultra-fast vacuum bladder mechanism

Pinguicula, commonly known as butterworts, have flat leaves covered with glandular cells that produce a sticky, greasy secretion. Small insects and even pollen grains become stuck to the surface. The leaves can slowly roll inward to maximize contact with captured prey. Many species also produce beautiful flowers resembling violets.
Wet rocky surfaces from the Arctic to tropical Mexico and the Alps
Flypaper trap – sticky glandular leaf surface with slow leaf movement

Darlingtonia californica, the cobra lily, is named for its remarkable resemblance to a rearing cobra snake. Uniquely among pitcher plants, it does not collect rainwater — it absorbs water through its roots from cold mountain streams. Translucent windows in the hood confuse trapped insects, causing them to exhaust themselves flying toward the false exits.
Cold mountain bogs and seeps in Oregon and northern California
Pitfall trap with false exits – translucent windows confuse prey
Albany pitcher plant, sole member of its family

Cephalotus follicularis, the Albany pitcher plant, is the sole member of its family and represents an independent evolution of carnivory. It is a small but remarkable plant producing both flat photosynthetic leaves and specialized pitcher-shaped leaves. Its pitchers are intricately structured with a ribbed, tooth-edged peristome and a protective lid to prevent rainwater dilution.
Peaty swamps near Albany, southwestern Australia
Pitfall trap – miniature pitcher with ribbed tooth-edged rim
